cf.title: MPTCP - multiplexing many TCP connections through one socket to get better bandwidth

input.subject: MPTCP - multiplexing many TCP connections through one socket to get better bandwidth

verdict_reasoning: The surviving level 1b objections, already-exists-1 and demand-1, decide this. Message #1 shows mptcpize giving the same multipath gain to unmodified binaries, and the thread names no setup that the wrapper cannot serve and no second user. The goal may be fine and the cost falls only on users who turn the feature on. So the result is "not now, show demand", resting on absence of evidence.

brief.title: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) support in the server and libpq on Linux
brief.problem: A single TCP connection is often capped below the available bandwidth, by per-flow limits in clouds (about 5 Gbps on many AWS and Azure VMs) or by WAN chokepoints. Every libpq connection uses one socket, so pg_basebackup, streaming and logical replication, COPY and postgres_fdw cannot use more than one flow. The workaround today is the mptcpize LD_PRELOAD wrapper, which the author calls inelegant.
brief.proposed_design: The postmaster opens its TCP listen sockets with IPPROTO_MPTCP when listen_mptcp is on, and libpq creates MPTCP client sockets when the mptcp option is set. The Linux kernel then spreads one application connection over several TCP subflows, and Postgres needs no other change. The support is Linux-only behind #ifdef IPPROTO_MPTCP, a GUC check hook rejects the setting where it is unsupported, and Unix-domain sockets ignore it.
user_visible_surface: Server GUC listen_mptcp (boolean, default off), placed in postgresql.conf.sample near client_connection_check_interval.
libpq connection option mptcp, default 0; only the value 1 turns it on in v5.
libpq environment variable PGMPTCP, same as the mptcp option.
libpq error message when MPTCP is requested on a TCP connection but not available.
author_claims: About 3 times faster \copy and pg_basebackup in a tc-limited test with 4 server MPTCP endpoints.
On AWS, iperf3 reached about 41 Gbps over one MPTCP stream, against 15-23 Gbps over one TCP stream.
Speeds up any libpq-based use with no other rework, and works with SSL/TLS (tested).
MPTCP is an IETF standard (RFC 8684) and is enabled by default in modern Linux distributions.
Built-in support is simpler than solving the bandwidth problem separately for each tool.
brief.thread_state: Greg Sabino Mullane, the only other participant, likes the idea and reviewed v4 for style, freeing, error messages, test lists and tests. v5 addresses his points, but the value syntax and a more generic listen_protocols / PGSOCKETPROTOCOL naming are still open.
unclear: Nobody besides the author has reported testing or benchmarking the patch.
The proposal does not say how the replication protocol and walreceiver connections get MPTCP, beyond libpq clients.
The proposal does not say how the server should report MPTCP use; pg_stat_mptcp was only floated.
The proposal does not say what happens when one side asks for MPTCP and the other has it disabled.
The minimal tests in 003_start_stop.pl do not show whether they check multipath behavior or only socket creation.
The proposal gives no plan for non-Linux platforms such as macOS or FreeBSD.

objections.title: mptcpize already gives MPTCP to unmodified Postgres and libpq clients
objections.failure_scenario: An operator who needs more than one flow can run `mptcpize run postgres ...` and `mptcpize run pg_basebackup ...` today and get the same subflows. Core then carries a GUC, a libpq option and an environment variable for a choice the kernel tooling already offers. That cost lasts for the life of the code.
objections.argument: Message #1 names mptcpize and dismisses it as "not elegant" because it needs edits to systemd startup scripts. That makes the existing way less convenient, but it does not show the job cannot be done. Message #1 also shows mptcpize running iperf3 with multipath gains, and the patch changes only the protocol argument to socket(), which is exactly what the wrapper overrides. A committer would likely ask what in-core placement adds beyond saving one wrapper line per service, and whether that gain is worth a permanent server and client setting.
objections.author_must_show: Which setup cannot be served by running the postmaster and clients under mptcpize, for example per-connection control in primary_conninfo or packaged clients you cannot wrap?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 itself shows mptcpize giving multipath gains, and its only stated drawback is editing systemd startup scripts. The thread names no setup that the wrapper cannot serve, so the inconvenience alone does not answer the objection.

objections.title: Demand rests on the author's own setup; mptcpize already covers it
objections.failure_scenario: An operator on a cloud VM sets PGMPTCP=1 and listen_mptcp=on and gets one subflow and no speedup. The kernel path manager needs `ip mptcp endpoint` and limits configured on both hosts, plus open firewall ports. Postgres would then own a GUC, a libpq option and an environment variable whose effect depends on host networking that it cannot see.
objections.argument: The demand evidence is the author's tc-limited demo, an iperf3 run and one production use from years ago (message #1, #2). One reviewer likes the idea but reports no testing (message #3, #6). The users who benefit already do root-level kernel MPTCP setup, so `mptcpize run` is a small extra step for them. Message #1 calls that wrapper inelegant, but it works today without any change to Postgres.
objections.author_must_show: Which users, besides the author, run or want MPTCP for pg_basebackup or replication, and what blocks them from using mptcpize today?

critic.reasoning: The cloud per-flow table in message #2 shows the limit is common, but the thread has no second user who wants MPTCP or has tested the patch. The mptcpize part repeats already-exists-1 and its no-speedup scenario does not bear on demand.

other_surviving.title: Boolean mptcp option with hard error breaks the libpq mode convention
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator puts PGMPTCP=1 in a shared profile or pg_service.conf, then runs psql from a macOS laptop or a Linux host with net.mptcp.enabled=0. libpq fails the connection with the new error message, so scripts that worked before stop at connect time on those hosts only.
other_surviving.argument: The brief lists an error when MPTCP is requested but not available. The only accepted value is '1', and message #7 leaves the spelling open. Transport choices in libpq that may be unavailable use modes such as sslmode and gssencmode, with prefer and require. A plain on/off option with a hard failure goes against that pattern, and the PGMPTCP name and its values cannot change after release.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should mptcp be a 0/1 flag that errors out, rather than a disable/prefer/require mode like gssencmode, given that MPTCP falls back to TCP in the kernel anyway?

critic.reasoning: The 0/1 spelling copies `keepalives`, so that part is existing practice. But libpq ignores keepalive settings where unsupported, while v5 fails the connection, and the thread gives no reason for the hard error.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: No way for users to see whether a connection uses MPTCP
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA sets listen_mptcp = on and mptcp=1 in primary_conninfo, but the path manager has no endpoints set up. The kernel falls back to one TCP subflow without notice, so replication runs no faster. pg_stat_replication and psql \conninfo give no sign of this.
other_surviving.argument: The setup steps in messages #1 and #2 depend on sysctl, ip mptcp limits and endpoints outside Postgres, so the most likely result of a wrong setup is silent plain TCP. pg_stat_ssl and pg_stat_gssapi report the transport they negotiate. Message #1 only floats a pg_stat_mptcp view as a contrib idea. The user-facing contract then has a switch with no matching view.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does a user find out, from the server or from psql, that a given connection actually runs over MPTCP and not plain TCP?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 only floats pg_stat_mptcp, and v5 touches no view or psql code. The kernel falls back to plain TCP without notice, so a user cannot confirm from Postgres that the setting took effect.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Network controls apply only to the first subflow of an MPTCP connection
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An admin limits Postgres to a private interface with listen_addresses and a host line in pg_hba.conf for 10.0.0.0/8. Kernel MPTCP endpoints, set up for another service, let later subflows join through a public interface, and session data travels over that path. The admin finds out only by inspecting traffic with ss -M or a packet capture.
other_surviving.argument: Authentication and logs use the peer address of the initial subflow. Subflows added later through MP_JOIN or ADD_ADDR can use other addresses and the extra ports shown in messages #1 and #2. Those ports are outside listen_addresses and are never checked against pg_hba.conf. The libpq.sgml hunk does not say this, and listen_mptcp turns on a system-wide kernel policy that the server does not see, so for a connection without TLS the data path can differ from what the admin configured.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Will the docs state that pg_hba.conf and listen_addresses cover only the initial subflow, and recommend TLS when subflows may use other paths?

critic.reasoning: MPTCP endpoints are set per network namespace, and later subflows can use addresses and ports that listen_addresses and pg_hba.conf never see. The libpq.sgml hunk does not mention this, and the request is a documentation note.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Transport-specific GUC and libpq option do not scale to later transports
refuted.failure_scenario: A later release adds QUIC or another transport the way message #7 suggests. It then needs listen_quic, a quic option and PGQUIC, plus rules for what happens when two are on at once. Users and tools such as poolers and drivers that parse conninfo must learn each new name.
refuted.argument: Message #7 already lists SCTP, QUIC and RDMA as possible next transports, and it leaves listen_protocols / PGSOCKETPROTOCOL open. Libpq connection options and environment variables are kept forever once released, so the name chosen now is permanent. Message #6 dropped the generic form because it cannot set a protocol per address family. That is a design question to settle before commit, and the same argument would apply to each later transport.
refuted.author_must_show: Which naming will hold if a second transport is added, and how would mptcp=1 then map onto it without a compatibility shim?

critic.reasoning: The scenario needs a hypothetical later transport, and one option per feature matches existing libpq practice (`sslmode`, `gssencmode`, `keepalives`). Message #6 weighed the generic name and dropped it because it cannot set a protocol per address family.

refuted.title: Behavior depends on kernel path-manager setup the project cannot test
refuted.failure_scenario: A user sets listen_mptcp = on and PGMPTCP=1 and gets no speedup, because no ip mptcp endpoint is set up or a firewall blocks the extra subflow ports. They report a Postgres bug. The buildfarm cannot reproduce it, and the 003_start_stop.pl test only shows that a socket opens.
refuted.argument: Messages #1 and #2 show that the gain needs sysctl limits, signal endpoints on extra ports and firewall changes on both hosts. Message #1 also says the kernel interface has changed and that mptcpd is still evolving. No one besides the author has tested the patch, and no committer has posted in the thread. Any later breakage in this area would fall on whichever committer pushes the patch.
refuted.author_must_show: What can the project test or document so that a no-speedup report is answered by setup steps rather than debugging the Postgres code?

critic.reasoning: A no-speedup report caused by missing `ip mptcp` endpoints or a firewall is a host setup problem, like routing, and the patch changes only the protocol argument to socket(). The visibility part duplicates standards-compat-2, and committer ownership belongs to committability.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Streaming and logical replication connections are named targets, so walsender and walreceiver sockets would run over MPTCP.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the boolean server GUC listen_mptcp, default off, with a check hook.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Later MPTCP subflows can use addresses and ports that listen_addresses and pg_hba.conf do not check.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The mptcp option, PGMPTCP and listen_mptcp become permanent names that depend on Linux kernel MPTCP behavior.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The mptcpize wrapper already gives MPTCP sockets to an unmodified postmaster and unmodified libpq clients.

questions: Which setup cannot be served by running the postmaster and clients under mptcpize, for example per-connection control in primary_conninfo or packaged clients that cannot be wrapped?
Which users, besides the author, run or want MPTCP for pg_basebackup or replication, and has anyone else tested or benchmarked the patch?
What happens to a connection when one side asks for MPTCP and the other side has it disabled or lacks kernel support?
How does a user find out, from the server or from psql, that a given connection runs over MPTCP and not plain TCP?
Why does mptcp=1 fail the connection where MPTCP is unavailable, when libpq ignores keepalive settings on platforms that do not support them?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the postmaster listen-socket code in pqcomm.c and the libpq connection code. No committer has posted in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for listen_mptcp, the mptcp option and PGMPTCP for as long as libpq exists. The owner also answers reports that depend on Linux kernel path-manager behavior, which the buildfarm cannot reproduce.
committability.author_follow_up: Good sign: the author revived the thread after a year, posted versions up to v5 that address review, and moved the entry through five CommitFests.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: Reports from independent users who need more than one flow for pg_basebackup or replication, plus a concrete setup where mptcpize does not work. An independent benchmark of the patch on a real cloud link would also help.

priority.reason: The patch is about 12 KiB, off by default and Linux-only, so cost falls on users who turn it on. It has been in 5 CommitFests with one reviewer and no committer, and the open point is demand beyond the author.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check whether keepalive and tcp_user_timeout socket options behave the same on MPTCP sockets. I also could not check whether the test in 003_start_stop.pl covers more than socket creation.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use AF_UNIX for tests on Windows (ie drop fallback TCP code)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Thomas Munro proposed using AF_UNIX sockets for pg_regress and TAP tests on Windows too, removing the Windows-only TCP and SSPI setup code in the test harness. To match Unix security, mkdtemp() on Windows would create the socket directory with access for the current user only.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that with TCP gone from the Windows tests, the TCP socket code would have little test coverage on any platform, and reviewers asked for a switch that runs the tests over either TCP or Unix sockets. The author agreed, set the TAP test patch aside for more work and posted only the first two patches. Those later stopped applying, the author posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If we remove that, won't we have a whole lot of code that's not
tested at all on any platform, ie all the TCP-socket code?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h"
Reverted commit(s): libpqwalreceiver: Convert to libpq-be-fe-helpers.h
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 728f86fec65537eade8d9e751961782ddb527934.

The signal handling was a few bricks shy of a load in that commit,
which made the walreceiver non-responsive to SIGTERM while it was
waiting for the connection to be established. That prevented a standby
from being promoted.

Since it was non-essential refactoring, let's revert it to make v16
work the same as earlier releases. I reverted it in 'master' too, to
keep the branches in sync. The refactoring was a good idea as such,
but it needs a bit more work. Once we have developed a complete patch
with this issue fixed, let's re-apply that to 'master'.

precedents_retrieved.title: socket_timeout in interfaces/libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a socket_timeout connection parameter to libpq so a client stops waiting and disconnects when a non-functional, overloaded server stops responding. The timeout was to be enforced inside pqWait(), the point where libpq clients can wait without end.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said earlier reviewers did not like an option that forces a cancellation on the connection. He also objected that a timeout in pqWait() skips the cleanup that pqDropConnection() normally does, since pqWait() is written never to time out. Reviewers did not engage further, and David Steele returned the patch, which no longer applied and still had no consensus.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Just with a quick look, assuming that you can bypass all
cleanup operations normally taken by pqDropConnection() through a
hijacking of pqWait() is not fine as this routine explicitely assumes
to *never* have a timeout for its wait.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds optional compression of libpq protocol traffic between client and server, using zlib or zstd, requested by the client with a connection-string option. Later versions negotiate algorithms through _pq_.compression in the startup packet, wrap compressed data in CompressedData messages, and let a libpq_compression server setting restrict the allowed algorithms and levels.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback because it had been waiting on author for two months. The last author message, in October 2021, promised lz4 support, but no new version followed after Daniel Gustafsson's rebase with a Windows build fix. Earlier review asked for a cleaned-up patch set, a fix for make check-world hangs with zlib, and code cleanup in the shared compression API.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch has been waiting on author for two months now, so I have
marked it as RwF in the CF app.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds optional streaming compression of libpq traffic (zlib, LZ4, and ZSTD in a second patch), negotiated through a _pq_.compression startup parameter and the new CompressionAck, CompressedData and SetCompressionMethod messages. A server setting, libpq_compression, controls the allowed algorithms, and each direction of traffic is compressed independently.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Jacob Champion marked the entry Returned with Feedback because it had waited on the author for longer than the two-week threshold. The last open review point came from Justin Pryzby in January 2022. He said compression still sat at the layer the 2019 thread had objected to, wrapping secure_read/write through function pointers instead of working inside them, where SSL is handled. The visible messages show no reply from the author to this point. Earlier review also asked for the server setting to default to off for security reasons, and reported an LZ4 assertion failure and CI test failures.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This entry has been waiting on author input for a while (our current threshold is roughly two weeks), so I've marked it Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add new protocol message to change GUCs to be able to change protocol extension parameters
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a protocol message that lets a client set a GUC without a SET command, so poolers can see the change and some parameters can be set only at the protocol level. Over time the work became a patch set with a protocol minor version bump, min_protocol_version and max_protocol_version libpq options, and protocol parameters such as report_parameters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry and moved the remaining protocol patches to the thread about longer cancel keys. Some pieces were committed here, including a libpq function PQfullProtocolVersion added in place of redefining PQprotocolVersion. The visible messages show no objection that rejected the core design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This required another rebase, but I've decided that I think it'll be most fruitful to continue the discussion on protocol changes in the thread about longer cancel keys[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: Use "protocol options" name instead of "protocol extensions" everywhere
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, Robert Haas, Jacob Champion, Laurenz Albe, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the term "protocol extensions" with "protocol options" in the docs and in a libpq error message, because "extension" suggests a link to Postgres extensions. No protocol options existed yet, so the author saw this as the time to settle on one name.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers did not agree on a new name. Heikki Linnakangas said "protocol option" suggests GUCs, Robert Haas found "protocol extensions" mildly clearer, Jacob Champion preferred keeping "protocol extension" with a docs note, and Laurenz Albe voted to keep "extension" because "option" already names other things in the docs. Peter Eisentraut rejected the patch for lack of consensus to change.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't think there is consensus for change, so I'm rejecting it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Password identifiers, protocol aging and SCRAM protocol
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set moves password storage from pg_authid into a new pg_auth_verifiers catalog, allowing one verifier per protocol per role, with a superuser GUC (password_protocols) and a sanitize function used by pg_upgrade to retire outdated protocols. On top of this it adds refactoring patches and SCRAM-SHA1 authentication as a new password protocol.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that the work should move to the next release cycle: these are large, user-facing changes involving wire protocol changes, and they had received little detailed code-level review. He judged that they could not be completed safely in the three weeks before feature freeze, and he questioned whether there was consensus on the direction, including multiple password verifiers. The author agreed that the SCRAM patch (0009) needed more time than remained, and no committer took it on; Magnus Hagander said he lacked time in this CommitFest. The author marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see how we're going to get all of this into 9.6, and these are big, user-facing changes that I don't think we should rush into under time pressure.

precedents_retrieved.title: Move libpq's write_failed mechanism down to pqsecure_raw_write().
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Move libpq's write_failed mechanism down to pqsecure_raw_write().
Reverted commit(s): Restructure libpq's handling of send failures.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 1f39a1c06 implemented write-failure postponement in pqSendSome,
which is above SSL/GSS processing.  However, we've now seen failures
indicating that (some versions of?) OpenSSL have a tendency to report
write failures prematurely too.  Hence, move the primary responsibility
for postponing write failures down to pqsecure_raw_write(), below
SSL/GSS processing.  pqSendSome now sets write_failed only in corner
cases where we'd lost the connection already.

A side-effect of this change is that errors detected in the SSL/GSS
layer itself will be reported immediately (as if they were read
errors) rather than being postponed like write errors.  That's
reverting an effect of 1f39a1c06, and I think it's fine: if there's
not a socket-level error, it's hard to be sure whether an OpenSSL
error ought to be considered a read or write failure anyway.

Another important point is that write-failure postponement is now
effective during connection setup.  OpenSSL's misbehavior of this
sort occurs during SSL_connect(), so that's a change we want.

Per bug #17391 from Nazir Bilal Yavuz.  Possibly this should be
back-patched, but I think it prudent to let it age awhile in HEAD
first.

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimize LISTEN/NOTIFY
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a shared-memory hash table that maps each channel to its listening backends, so NOTIFY signals only those backends instead of every listener in the database. Later versions replaced this with a per-backend atomic state machine and SetLatch wakeups, so notifiers skip signals to backends that already have one pending.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patches. He said the latest version only removes redundant IPC signals and does not fix the scalability problems, and that this work could be done outside async.c through the ProcSignal or "Interrupts vs signals" work. He also named the heavyweight lock in PreCommit_Notify() as a second bottleneck and asked others how to proceed before going on with the per-channel listener tracking.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm withdrawing the latest patches, since they won't fix the scalability
problems, but only provide some performance improvements by eliminating
redundant IPC signalling.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P6] and [P7] are libpq compression patches, a different idea, and both were returned because the author did not follow up, a reason that does not apply here. The thread cites no earlier MPTCP discussion. Message #2 links a separate pg_basebackup patch only for benchmark numbers.

Greg's generic listen_protocols naming point was withdrawn by him in message #6, so it is not raised. The check hook that rejects listen_mptcp on unsupported platforms follows existing practice (check_bonjour), so it is not raised either.

The proposal adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog or protocol-message state; MPTCP changes only the socket protocol, and the kernel falls back to plain TCP. Not checked without code: whether keepalive and tcp_user_timeout socket options behave the same on MPTCP sockets on walsender and walreceiver connections.

The defaults are safe: listen_mptcp is off and can be set only by an admin. The client option only changes the client's own socket, so I see no path for privilege escalation or denial of service beyond the kernel's subflow limits.
